title: Present value of a series of cash flows
summary: Discounting a stream of amounts year by year: equal amounts, uneven amounts, and choosing an SUV advertising plan.

chunks.heading: The formula for a stream of amounts
chunks.explanation_md:
Often you get money not once but **at the end of each period for n periods**. The **present value of a series** simply discounts each amount by its own number of years and adds them up:

**PV = FV₁ / (1 + i)^1 + FV₂ / (1 + i)^2 + ... + FVₙ / (1 + i)^n**

The slide also writes this compactly as a sum (Σ) from t = 1 to n: each year's amount FVₜ divided by (1 + i) raised to t.

The key idea: **money further in the future is divided by a bigger number**, so it counts for less today.

key_terms.meaning: Present value of a stream of future amounts (FVₜ) received at the end of each period for n periods: the sum of each amount divided by (1 + i)^t.

chunks.exam_line: PV of a series = FV₁/(1 + i)^1 + FV₂/(1 + i)^2 + ... + FVₙ/(1 + i)^n.

chunks.heading: Equal amounts: $1,000 a year for 3 years at 6%
chunks.explanation_md:
**Question:** you will receive **$1,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years**. The interest rate is **6%**. What is the present value?

**Given:** FV = 1000, i = 6%, n = 3.

**Working:**

PV = 1000/(1 + 0.06)^1 + 1000/(1 + 0.06)^2 + 1000/(1 + 0.06)^3 = **$2,673**

Notice: you receive $3,000 in total, but it is worth only $2,673 today, because the later payments are discounted more.
chunks.exam_line: $1,000 at the end of each of 3 years at 6%: PV = $2,673.

chunks.heading: Uneven amounts: four different cash flows at 8%
chunks.explanation_md:
**Question:** a project gives **uneven year-end cash flows**: **$1,500 (Year 1), $2,200 (Year 2), $1,800 (Year 3) and $2,600 (Year 4)**. At **8%**, what is the present value?

The method is exactly the same; only the numerators change.

**Given:** FV = 1500, 2200, 1800, 2600; i = 8%; n = 4.

**Working:**

PV = 1500/(1.08)^1 + 2200/(1.08)^2 + 1800/(1.08)^3 + 2600/(1.08)^4 = **$6,615.01**

chunks.heading: Case: which SUV advertising intensity maximizes firm value?
chunks.explanation_md:
**Practice question:** you are the marketing manager for a major automaker choosing an **advertising intensity for a new SUV**. Expected year-end profits ($ millions), with an **opportunity cost of funds of 10 percent**:

| Advertising Intensity | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| High | 20 | 95 | 275 |
| Moderate | 35 | 80 | 155 |
| Low | 75 | 110 | 130 |

**Solution: discount each year's profit back at 10% and sum.**

- **High:** PV = 20/(1.10)^1 + 95/(1.10)^2 + 275/(1.10)^3 = **$303.3** million
- **Moderate:** PV = 35/(1.10)^1 + 80/(1.10)^2 + 155/(1.10)^3 = **$214.39** million
- **Low:** PV = 75/(1.10)^1 + 110/(1.10)^2 + 130/(1.10)^3 = **$256.76** million

**Ranking:** High ($303.31M) > Low ($256.76M) > Moderate ($214.39M).

**Decision:** **high advertising intensity maximizes the present value of the firm**, even though it has the lowest profits in Years 1-2. The much larger Year 3 payoff more than compensates once discounted. **Always compare full discounted streams, not single-year snapshots.**
chunks.exam_line: SUV case: High ($303.31M) > Low ($256.76M) > Moderate ($214.39M); compare full discounted streams, not single-year snapshots.

questions.stem: As marketing manager for a major automaker, you must choose an advertising intensity for a new SUV. Expected year-end profits ($ millions) are: High 20, 95, 275; Moderate 35, 80, 155; Low 75, 110, 130 for Years 1 to 3. The opportunity cost of funds is 10 percent. Which intensity maximizes the value of the firm? Show full working and comment.
questions.model_answer_md:
Profits arrive in different years, so we must compare their present values, not the raw figures.

**Formula:** PV = FV_1/(1 + i)^1 + FV_2/(1 + i)^2 + FV_3/(1 + i)^3, with i = 10%. The divisors are 1.10, (1.10)^2 = 1.21 and (1.10)^3 = 1.331.

**Working ($ millions):**

| Intensity | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | PV |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High | 20/1.10 ≈ 18.18 | 95/1.21 ≈ 78.51 | 275/1.331 ≈ 206.61 | **303.31** |
| Moderate | 35/1.10 ≈ 31.82 | 80/1.21 ≈ 66.12 | 155/1.331 ≈ 116.45 | **214.39** |
| Low | 75/1.10 ≈ 68.18 | 110/1.21 ≈ 90.91 | 130/1.331 ≈ 97.67 | **256.76** |

**Ranking:** High ($303.31M) > Low ($256.76M) > Moderate ($214.39M).

**Decision:** choose **high advertising intensity**; it **maximizes the present value of the firm**.

**Comment:**
- High has the **lowest profits in Years 1 and 2**, and Low looks best in those years.
- But High's **much larger Year 3 payoff more than compensates once discounted**.
- A manager who looked only at the early years would pick the wrong option.

**Conclusion:** **always compare full discounted streams, not single-year snapshots**. Because the firm's value is the present value of its profits, the option with the highest PV is the one that maximizes firm value.

questions.stem: Differentiate between the present value of a single amount and the present value of a series of cash flows. Illustrate each with the session's examples.
questions.model_answer_md:
Both bring future money back to today, but one handles a single payment and the other a stream of payments.

| Basis | PV of a single amount | PV of a series |
|---|---|---|
| What is received | One amount, FV, after n periods | An amount FV_t **at the end of each period for n periods** |
| Formula | **PV = FV / (1 + i)^n** | **PV = FV_1/(1 + i)^1 + FV_2/(1 + i)^2 + ... + FV_n/(1 + i)^n** |
| Steps | One division | Discount each amount by its own year, then add |
| Amounts | Just one | Can be **equal** or **uneven** |

**Example of a single amount.** You receive **₹1,100 after a year** at **10%**: PV = 1,100 / (1 + 0.10) = **₹1,000**.

**Examples of a series.**
- **Equal amounts:** $1,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years at 6%: PV = 1000/(1.06)^1 + 1000/(1.06)^2 + 1000/(1.06)^3 = **$2,673**.
- **Uneven amounts:** $1,500, $2,200, $1,800 and $2,600 in Years 1 to 4 at 8%: PV = 1500/(1.08)^1 + 2200/(1.08)^2 + 1800/(1.08)^3 + 2600/(1.08)^4 = **$6,615.01**.

**The link.** A series is just several single amounts added together: each term in the series formula is the single-amount formula with its own n. In every case, money further away is divided by a bigger number and counts for less.

**Conclusion:** use the single-amount formula for one payment and the series formula for a stream; the logic of discounting is the same in both.

questions.model_answer_md:
Each payment is discounted by its own number of years and the results are added.

**Formula:** PV = FV_1/(1 + i)^1 + FV_2/(1 + i)^2 + ... + FV_n/(1 + i)^n

**Given:** FV = 1000; i = 6%; n = 3.

**Working:**
- Year 1: 1000/(1.06)^1 ≈ 943.40
- Year 2: 1000/(1.06)^2 ≈ 890.00

questions.stem: A project gives year-end cash flows of $1,500, $2,200, $1,800 and $2,600 in Years 1 to 4. At 8%, find the present value of this uneven stream.
questions.model_answer_md:
The method for uneven flows is the same as for equal ones; only the numerators change.

**Formula:** PV = FV_1/(1 + i)^1 + FV_2/(1 + i)^2 + FV_3/(1 + i)^3 + FV_4/(1 + i)^4

**Given:** FV = 1500, 2200, 1800, 2600; i = 8%; n = 4.

**Working:**
- 1500/(1.08)^1 ≈ 1,388.89
- 2200/(1.08)^2 ≈ 1,886.15
- 1800/(1.08)^3 ≈ 1,428.90
- 2600/(1.08)^4 ≈ 1,911.08
- **PV = $6,615.01** (adding the unrounded values)

**Comment:** the stream is worth $6,615.01 today; uneven flows just need each year discounted separately.

questions.stem: Explain the present value of a series and why each amount is discounted by its own number of years.
questions.model_answer_md:
Many decisions pay out not once but **at the end of each period for n periods**.

- **Present value of a series:** discount each future amount back to today and add them up.
- **Formula:** **PV = FV_1/(1 + i)^1 + FV_2/(1 + i)^2 + ... + FV_n/(1 + i)^n**, also written as a sum from t = 1 to n.
- **Own number of years:** money received in year t waits t years, so it is divided by (1 + i)^t. The further away, the **bigger the divisor**, and the less it counts today.

**Example:** $1,000 a year for 3 years at 6% is worth **$2,673** today, not $3,000.

So a series is valued by discounting each amount separately, never by adding raw amounts.
